pr_title: Run all OnExit before all OnEnter
pr_body:
Fixes #10732. Copying description from that issue.

# Objective

`StateTransition` schedule executes `apply_state_transition` system for each state in order. `apply_state_transition` executes `OnExit`, `OnTransition`, `OnEnter` schedules in order.

https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/blob/4eafd60ce9dd3dd579c07798ceb43f88a13d7094/crates/bevy_ecs/src/schedule/state.rs#L154-L161

This is somewhat inconvenient.

For example, application state can be controller by two state types, `StateA` and `StateB` (for example, state and substate).

Each state may want to for example, set cursor icon on enter and reset it to default on exit (clean up). This is not possible now, because cleanup of second system (`OnExit`) can be executed after init of first system (`OnEnter`).

## Solution

Execute systems in order:

```rust
OnExit<A>
OnExit<B>
OnTransition<A>
OnTransition<B>
OnEnter<A>
OnEnter<B>
```

## Changelog

- Deprecate `apply_state_transition::<T>` system
- Add `apply_state_transition_on_exit::<T>`, `apply_state_transition_on_transition::<T>`, `apply_state_transition_on_enter::<T>` systems
- Add non-generic `AfterOnExit`, `BeforeOnEnter` labels to order the systems

## Migration Guide

No migration needed if only one state was used which was initialized with `.add_state`.

If more than one state is used, order of state callback execution was changed, need to review the code to make sure it is not broken.

If `apply_state_transition` system was used directly, it will still work, but this function is deprecated and will be eventually removed.

## Side note

I proposed implicit system ordering (#10678, #10618) before, and I think this is another illustration where implicit ordering would be beneficial.

In current setup (before or after this PR) all systems are exclusive and thus not parallel. I imagine it could be like this:

```rust
app.add_systems(
  ScheduleTransition,
  enter_main_menu.on_enter(GameState::MainMenu),
)
```

~~`enter_main_menu.on_enter(GameState::MainMenu)` could create a system with after-dependency on non-generic `BeforeOnEnter`.~~ **Edit**: actually we can already do that, by adding the same before/after as this diff does.

So all the systems in `ScheduleTransition` will run concurrently, but with proper ordering, no subschedules.

Moreover, we would not even need to run `enter_main_menu` in `ScheduleTransition`, we could run it in `Update` (or any other schedule), if we could implicitly order all regular systems which read or update state after all systems which are triggered on state change.

But that is somewhat offtopic here. For now I mostly want to deal with this ordering issue.
pr_comments: Now all the transition systems observe consistent states of every state (not just own).

If you're worried about overhead from adding all these extra systems, we can eliminate most of that by adding run conditions to the `on_exit`, `on_transition`, and `on_enter` systems, which will prevent the executor from even spawning a task for these systems unless a state transition is happening. If we attach the run condition to a system set, then it will only be evaluated once for each state type which avoids even more overhead.

@JoJoJet like this?

```rust
            .add_systems(
                StateTransition,
                (
                    apply_state_transition_before_transition::<S>
                        .in_set(StateTransitionSet::BeforeTransition),
                    apply_state_transition_on_exit::<S>.in_set(StateTransitionSet::OnExit),
                    apply_state_transition_on_transition::<S>
                        .in_set(StateTransitionSet::OnTransition),
                    apply_state_transition_on_enter::<S>.in_set(StateTransitionSet::OnEnter),
                    apply_state_transition_after_transition::<S>
                        .in_set(StateTransitionSet::AfterTransition),
                // HERE
                ).run_if(next_state_was_updated::<T>),
            );
```

Should I do it in this PR or in follow-up?
That's a lot simpler than what I was picturing, but yeah that should work perfectly. Just make it check if `Res<NextState>` is `Some`
Might as well make the change in this PR since it's quite small.

Rewritten some code:
* five systems are now guarded by a common condition
* systems made private and instead `apply_state_transition_systems` function exposes them
* each those systems now assume states are correct instead of checking state
* added state `StateTransitionSet::RunEnterOnce` to make first on-enter also safe
Removed `World` in `apply_before_transition` and `apply_after_transition`.
Another iteration of applying suggestions done.
Thank you!

Is anything else needed to be done to merge this PR?

Making code work correctly with multiple states is tedious for scenarios I explained: set up something when entering state, and cleanup when leaving state need to be done very carefully when state enter/exit are executed in unknown order.
Previously we were waiting on two approvals from SMEs, but I suppose we have  those now. @alice-i-cecile,  think we should merge this?
@maniwani @hymm I'd like a last set of opinions from at least one of you. I'm nervous there's something I'm missing. The loss of atomicity is annoying, but I think that the benefits are worth it.

I'm ambivalent about this PR. It does make things a little nicer by making the ordering predictable, but what we really need is a solution for sub states and this doesn't feel like it gets us any closer to that. This has an incorrect ordering for sub states. i.e. If `B` is a substate of `A` the correct ordering ignoring the transition schedules is `OnEnter<A>`, `OnEnter<B>`, `OnExit<B>`, `OnExit<A>`. This is so all the B state is cleaned up before trying to exit the A state. So when states have a dependency on each other they have an inside outside relationship with each other. The ordering described in this pr is just arbitrary. But arbitrary is probably better than random. But this is a lot of complexity over the previous code, so I could go either way.

One question I have is what would adding a state to the render schedule look like after this PR?

> what we really need is a solution for sub states

Also it can actually built on top of that. Relatively simple API, and more or less compatible with current, might be:

```rust
trait States {
  // New member.
  // Generated by proc macro.
  type ParentState: States;
}

#[derive(States)]
#[state(parent = A)] // Optional.
enum B { ... }
```

And then in new `apply_state_transition_systems` we need to add more constraints for the state relative to parent sets. For example,

```rust
run_enter_schedule::<S>.in_set(StateTransitionSet::OnEnter)
```

should become something like

```rust
run_enter_schedule::<S>
  .in_set(StateTransitionSet::OnEnter)
  .after(run_enter_schedule::<S::ParentState>) // this should add dependency only is S != S::ParentState
```

This would just set state transitions correctly ordered relative to parent.

Now we have ordering of enter/exit.

**The tricky part is automatically change parent state and child states when current state changes**. This would be harder, I have some ideas how to do it, but it would be a wall of text. But the bottom line is:

> this doesn't feel like it gets us any closer to that

It gets us a little closer to that:
- It adds some constraints which must be preserved when substates implemented
- It adds a test which must still pass if states are hierarchical

> I'd like a last set of opinions from at least one of you. I'm nervous there's something I'm missing. The loss of atomicity is annoying, but I think that the benefits are worth it.

Is this PR motivated by sub-states? It's not super clear to me what the goal or benefit here is.

> What we really need is a solution for sub-states and this doesn't feel like it gets us any closer to that.
> [Sub-states] have an inside-outside relationship with each other. The ordering described in this PR is just arbitrary. 

I tend to agree. I would prefer to handle that with observers (e.g. #10839). The way observers "splice" new commands into the overall queue would give us the stack/recursion we need to make nested state transitions happen in the desired order.

This is kind of a side note, but I'm ambivalent about our convention of running all transitions in a single place in `Main`. If we could adopt a convention where parent-child is the only relationship we acknowledge between states, then (with observers) there would be no issue with individual state transitions taking effect "immediately" (next sync point).

> Is this PR motivated by sub-states?

Yes, I use substates in my app (but it is complex and not scalable implementation).

<details>
<summary>For the record, this is what I do now.</summary>

There are several states in my "game". Let's call them:
- we are building a house
  - we are picking a place to build a house
  - we are choosing the house size
- we are hovering over the entities on the map
- various unknown states like "doing nothing" or "console open" or "main menu" or "building something else I didn't fully implement yet"

When known state is entered in one of known states, the application:
- changes cursor
- changes help panel on the screen

When known state is exited, the application:
- resets cursor to default
- clear help panel

Unknown state enter/exit has nothing to do with cursor or panel.

So when state is unknown, we don't leave cursor and help in previous state.

Currently I implemented this logic as: there's a resource like

```
#[derive(Resource, Default)]
struct WantCursor {
  want_cursor: Cursor,
  clear_cursor: bool,
}
```

and there's a system:

```
fn update_cursor_on_request_after_state_changes(
  cursor: ResMut<WantCursor>
) {
  if cursor.is_changed() {
    if cursor.want_cursor {
      // actually set cursor
    } else {
      // reset cursor to default
    }
    *cursor = WantCursor::default();
  }
}
```

So `OnEnter` of known state cursor resource `want_cursor` is set. And `OnExit` `clear_cursor` is set. So if both `OnEnter` and `OnExit` run, both `want_cursor` and `clear_cursor` are set, but `want_cursor` has precedence.

If all `OnExit` were executed before all `OnEnter`, I would not need this `clear_cursor`/extra system hacks, and could set/clear the cursor right in `OnEnter`/`OnExit`.
</details>

> I'm ambivalent about our convention of running all transitions in a single place in `Main`

I actually think this is drawback of current design. Instead we could schedule all the systems which depend on the state after all the `OnEnter`/`OnExit` systems — probably even in `Update` schedule — to increase parallelism.

I raised this issue numerous times (last time, [here](https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/discussions/10851)) and was not understood.

> I would prefer to handle that with observers (e.g. https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/pull/10839)

I read this PR.
- It is about entities, not resources
- PR description does not say anything about order
- Observers seem to access the world, so no parallelism? Seems to be drawback.
- Overall, seems not very related to this issue. But maybe I probably did not understand it.

> - It is about entities, not resources.

No, it's not. The PR gives examples with structural change events like `OnAdd`, but users can define their own events to emit (see the `Resize` example). Just know that specifying a `target` is optional. A user could emit an event with no particular target and have observers listening for that.

Being able to register callbacks on internal ECS changes is just one of the benefits of observers, not their sole purpose.

> - PR description does not say anything about order.

I have insider knowledge. Just take my word for it. If commands `A` and `B` are queued and `A` runs and does something that triggers observers, any commands those produce (and so on, "recursively") will run before `B`.

> - Observers seem to access the world, so no parallelism?

Correct.[^1]

> Seems to be drawback.

The status quo is that different states do not transition in parallel. They *can't* transition in parallel because those are distinct schedules (dependency graphs), and the reasons why *that* is the case are: 

- State transitions can make structural changes. There were no reasons to consider letting multiple transitions overlap. (No clue if we think differently now, but definitely not back then.)
- States are allowed to transition in any schedule and even at multiple points in the same schedule.[^2] A key conclusion of the scheduling V3 work was that the dependency graph can't represent cycles (obvious, I know) or branches. Doing flow control requires exclusive access (i.e. you can only loop/branch *inside* a command or an exclusive system).
  
Maybe there's an alternative where we say there's a singular, all-encompassing "app state" with two singular "enter" and "exit" schedules owning the systems from all user states (with `OnEnter(S)` and `OnExit(S)` as sets) that we run for *any* transition. idk

[^1]: I think the community values "running systems in parallel" too highly. Parallel system execution has pretty significant overhead and we lack solid evidence that it handily wins against the more basic, serial execution.

[^2]: This is partly why I brought up observers and also why I'm ambivalent about this unique property of the `Main` schedule. `Main` having one spot where transitions are supposed to happen was an executive decision.

> They can't transition in parallel because those are distinct schedules

I would actually prefer to change that. Instead of API

```
app.add_systems(OnEnter(X), enter_x)
```

I would have API

```
app.add_on_enter(X, enter_x)
```

so Bevy would have more freedom to change state internals. In particular, all the systems will be arranged relative to each other just with system sets.

> I think the community values "running systems in parallel" too highly

It is an interesting topic.

I think this is not what community "values", but this is what community "expects".

For example, if execution is multi-threaded
- I make sure a system does not grab more than it needs to (to allow other heavy systems run concurrently with it)
- I'm careful about not adding unnecessary dependencies to the systems
- at the same time I avoid optimizations of heavy systems, because machine is busy running other heavy systems anyway

If Bevy main schedule was single threaded, I could live with it, but it would significantly change my coding style, for example:
- I would not worry about grabbing too many resources mutably
  - in particular, I would probably add a param like `EasyParamEverythingMyGameEverMayNeed`
- generally I would make systems larger to simplicity of coding (because it does not affect main schedule execution time)
- at the same time I would start parallelizing work inside the systems, because each system is now now critical path

Basically, single-threaded vs multithreaded imply very different coding styles. Either is probably fine.

If Bevy advertises multi-threaded setup, it needs to make sure it utilizes this multi-threading as much as possible. In particular, in state transitions and things such observers.

Maybe Bevy should stop doing that.

I have rewritten my app with custom state implementation, so I don't need this PR as much as before.

Closing to reduce the queue size. If something changes their mind and thinks it would be good idea to merge it, please ping me, and I'll reopen it and rebase.
@stepancheg This seems like an important PR for sake of consistency if nothing else; it helps the graph make more sense.

issue_context.title: Run all OnExit before all OnEnter
issue_context.body:
`StateTransition` schedule executes `apply_state_transition` system for each state in order. `apply_state_transition` executes `OnExit`, `OnTransition`, `OnEnter` schedules in order.

https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/blob/4eafd60ce9dd3dd579c07798ceb43f88a13d7094/crates/bevy_ecs/src/schedule/state.rs#L154-L161

This is somewhat inconvenient.

For example, application state can be controller by two state types, `StateA` and `StateB` (for example, state and substate).

Each state may want to for example, set cursor icon on enter and reset it to default on exit (clean up). This is not possible now, because cleanup of second system (`OnExit`) can be executed after init of first system (`OnEnter`).

Propose to execute systems in order:

```
OnExit<A>
OnExit<B>
OnTransition<A>
OnTransition<B>
OnEnter<A>
OnEnter<B>
```
comments:
Hmm 🤔 I'm not sure we can easily do this: the `apply_state_transitions` system is generic over a single state.

And without "trait queries for resources" or something, I don't have a good sense of how we'd do this in general.

> I'm not sure we can easily do this

Split `apply_split_transition` into three systems, add them separately, add common (non-generic) dependency between them: add two `SystemSet` labels (`AfterOnExit`, `BeforeOnEnter`) and schedule like this:

```rust
.add_systems(
  StateTransition,
  (
    apply_on_enter::<S>.before(AfterOnExit),
    apply_on_transition::<S>.after(AfterOnExit).before(BeforeOnEnter),
    apply_on_enter::<S>.after(BeforeOnEnter)
  )
)
```

Oh clever: that's a good architecture. I need to think a bit more about whether this is a *good* idea to do still.

I can see your point in the original issue, but by breaking it apart, you lose atomicity of the state transitions.

Currently it's Very Hard to see / interact with the world when a state is in an in-between state. Which is obviously helpful for correctness and modularity.

I think this schedule execution order would be more consistent than what we have now. The instances of `apply_state_transition` in the `StateTransition` schedule have no fixed run order, which means if you have a system that runs `OnEnter<A>` and accesses `Res<State<B>>`, there's no guarantee if the system will run before or after `B`'s state transition, and it might even change order from frame to frame.

That said, wanting atomicity is a good point. If you put a call to `apply_state_transition<A>` inside of an `OnEnter<B>` schedule, it would break `A`, which may not be obvious. Then again, nesting calls to `apply_state_transition` might be asking to have your code broken.

I think reordering the scheduling this way is a huge win. 
It should be much easier to document the expected behavior and thus reason about what is happening. 

I feel like having Atomic transitions has less value than a clearly defined order for interleaving different state transitions. 

Ideally if you have two different states they should be as decoupled as possible. 
If it is really critical for StateA, to be able to reason about what StateB is doing, then I think the user should add explicit orderings between the transition schedules (like enforcing `OnExit(Substate)` before `OnExit(SuperState)`).

How about introducing StateSet that works atomically for different state sets like as is but batches the state application within the same state sets.
I encountered this in my current project. In my case, it's a problem that, after changing two different state A and B in the same time, a system OnExit(A::Something) gets the old value of B. So I've created a custom state system tailered for the states A and B, that works in a way like the one suggested in here. But I noticed it can be generalized to any states.
I know the atomicity is somewhat convenient in some cases, but a sync point for different states is a critical requirement in my case. StateSet gives us an opt-in option to have a sync point for specific states.

This is fixed in [pyri_state](https://github.com/benfrankel/pyri_state) by allowing you to specify dependencies between states:

```rust
#[derive(State, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
#[state(before(B))]
struct A;

#[derive(State, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
// You can specify the dependency here instead: #[state(after(A))]
struct B;
```

Then their system sets will run in the `StateFlush` schedule in this order:

```
StateFlushSet::<A>::Resolve
  StateFlushSet::<A>::Trigger
  StateFlushSet::<A>::Flush
    StateFlushSet::<A>::Exit
    StateFlushSet::<A>::Transition
    StateFlushSet::<A>::Enter

...

StateFlushSet::<B>::Resolve
  StateFlushSet::<B>::Trigger
  StateFlushSet::<B>::Flush
    StateFlushSet::<B>::Exit
    StateFlushSet::<B>::Transition
    StateFlushSet::<B>::Enter
```

Or you can manually specify any ordering requirements you want by configuring the system sets yourself.

I'm pretty sure this was fixed in the last states rewrite.
All states in the state machine DAG will trigger their schedules correctly:
- on exit - top to bottom
- on transition - unspecified
- on enter - bottom to top

If states aren't directly related it's hard to talk about any sort of ordering.
@benfrankel can you confirm/deny? It's been a while.

Yes, `bevy_state` runs all exit schedules before running any enter schedules now (via the `StateTransitionSteps` system sets), with additional ordering based on substates (via the `ExitSchedules<S>` and `EnterSchedules<S>` system sets).

The approach taken in `pyri_state` is an alternate solution, but both approaches resolve this issue.

review_comments: We can probably unset this after calling `OnTransition`

Aren't you as paranoid about performance of running extra system per state 60 times per second as I am?

Probably it is nothing, but this is the only argument I have against running it as a separate system after `on_enter`. From design point of view, this would be best.
System overhead is quite cheap: I would aim for correctness first.
This should be a deprecation warning.
